newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: FOCUS - Venezuela bank ruling seen as beneficial.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Venezuela bank ruling seen as beneficial.

text.p: A ruling that Venezuelan state-owned banks must meet the central bank's reserve requirements will help them prepare for eventual privatisation and help the country damp inflation, analysts said.

"The first objective looks to be to prepare state-owned banks for privatisation -- previously they were not burdened with the reserve requirement," said Metroeconomica economist Jose Barcia. "But clearly it will also have a good effect on inflation," he added.

State-owned Banco Venezuela, Banco Consolidado and Banco Latino are all slated for privatisation before the end of the year as part of a wider sell-off of assets that the government assumed during the country's 1994-95 banking crisis.
According to the ruling, state-owned banks will have to place two percent of their deposits in non-interest-bearing accounts at the central bank.

That rate will rise gradually every month until it reaches the 12 percent rate currently required of private banks. The decree, published in Tuesday's official gazette that records government legislation, takes effect December 2.

"One question is, are these banks now ready -- healthy enough -- to assume the burden of reserve requirements?" said Barcia. "Presumably they are judged to be so, although the move to the full 12 percent reserve-requirement rate is wisely gradual."

State-owned banks currently account for about a quarter of the country's total bank deposits, which totalled 3.858 trillion bolivars ($8.2 billion) in September, according to the financial magazine VenEconomy.
If 12 percent of their deposits were suddenly placed in the central bank, liquidity would drop. "That would have a huge impact on interest rates," said New York-based IDEA analyst Gene Freida.

As interest rates surged, the price of government bonds and other securities would plunge, which could prompt a sell-off by Venezuelan banks, which currently hold around 40 percent of their portfolios in such fixed-income securities, Freida said.
"Clearly it is much more sensible to phase it in, especially as seasonal demand for bolivars is rising ahead of Christmas," he added.
Lowering or raising reserve requirements effectively influences the money supply, and thus inflation.

Analysts were surprised when October inflation rose to 4.2 percent. Although November inflation is expected to fall back to around 3.0 percent, that is still more than the government's original year-end target of between 1.5 and 2.0 percent, part of its agreement with the International Monetary Fund.
